founder.name: Andrew Hayes
founder.headline: The 99-1 Rule: Your next fifty customers are already on LinkedIn. Get them with stories that grab their attention.

lm.title: The 99-1 Story Checklist: 7 Questions Before You Hit Publish
lm.promise: Answer all seven and your post stops the 99% who weren't looking for you, before they know they need what you sell.
whats_inside: Is there a real person at the center of this, with a name, a job, and a daily routine?
What was that person actually doing on LinkedIn the moment this story found them?
Have you named their obstacle before your brand appears anywhere in the post?
Is your brand the guide in this story, not the hero?
Is the setting specific enough that the reader can picture themselves in it?
Does the post end without a pitch, a CTA, or a product mention?
Would someone scroll past your company name and still stop to finish reading?

posts.body:
She called me on a Tuesday, about twenty minutes after I sent the file.

She'd just finished reading through the results from her CueVu pilot. The file had the responses of dozens of real people from a consumer panel, people who recently switched brands in her product category. Her exact future customers, before they knew her brand existed.

We asked each one the same question. What were you feeling when it happened?

They answered in their own words. You could trace the reasoning in each response, the way the frustration built up.

She said she had no idea her buyers thought about the decision this way. She meant people who hadn't found her yet.

The file is dozens of real stories, written in the language your future customers actually use. Every person in it is a post waiting to happen.

The pilot starts at $295.

posts.body:
After a few stories run, I ask the client to look at who came back.

These readers were never searching for a solution. They read one post, and then showed up for the next. By the time a few are out, LinkedIn has learned who slows down for your content and started putting the next story in front of the same people automatically.

Every story you share leaves those readers thinking a little differently than they did before. None of it requires a pitch.

As the storyteller, you can tease what's coming next at the end of each one, a detail left open or a result you haven't gotten to yet. The people who read the last story come back for the next one. An audience builds from readers waiting for the continuation, and most of them were never in the market when they found you.

posts.body:
95% of AI-generated marketing campaigns had no measurable return.

That's MIT's finding, across $40 billion in spend.

Forty billion dollars against a zero return, and Salesforce's Bobby Jania put the explanation in one sentence: we are using the most powerful technology in history to send more one-way spam, faster.

There are 134 million active LinkedIn users every day. Average visit is 8 minutes. 99% of them came to check on people they know, who got promoted or changed jobs. Sending more content they didn't ask for doesn't close that gap.

LinkedIn's algorithm now reads for meaning, buries the generic, and surfaces real stories told in real customer language. The timing makes sense.
posts.hook: 95% of AI-generated marketing campaigns had no measurable return.

follow_ups.body: You have the 99-1 checklist. Seven questions, but question 3 does the most work: naming the obstacle before your brand shows up anywhere in the post. Get that right and the reader feels seen before they know who you are. Run your next draft through that one first, then work outward.
follow_ups.subject: Your checklist (start with question 3)

follow_ups.body: Getting the person right at question 1 comes quickly. The setting is the harder one. "In a coffee shop" is a placeholder. "Reviewing a contract she'd already sent back twice" is a scene, and that difference is exactly what question 5 is testing.
follow_ups.subject: The setting question is trickier than it looks
